steps.title: Yes, farther — and still hotter
steps.say: Good catch: in northern summer Earth is actually near its farthest point from the Sun. So distance can't be the cause.

ops.text:
Right: northern summer is near Earth's
FARTHEST point from the Sun.
So distance is not the cause.

steps.title: Sunlight hits at an angle
steps.say: What changes is the angle of the sunlight. A tilted Earth makes the northern half face the Sun more directly in summer.

ops.text:
The tilt changes the ANGLE of sunlight:
steeper rays = more concentrated heat.

steps.title: Summer side vs winter side
steps.say: On the left, the north pole leans toward the Sun — northern summer. On the right, it leans away — northern winter.

steps.title: Same rays, spread out
steps.say: Steep rays pack energy into a small area; slanted rays spread the same energy over a larger area, so it is weaker.

ops.text:
slanted rays:
same energy, larger area, cooler

steps.title: Longer days too
steps.say: Summer also brings longer days, so the ground has more hours to warm up.

ops.text:
Plus: summer days are longer,
so more hours of heating.

steps.title: The takeaway
steps.say: Seasons come from the 23.5 degree tilt — the angle of sunlight and day length — not from our distance to the Sun.
